headline: Race Rock at 3.6 Knots: Bass Down Deep, Blues Stacked at the Thames
subhead: Warm Sound water has the trophy bass hugging bottom on wire line, but the Thames mouth is loaded with snapper blues and the sea bass bite on Plum Gut structure is the week's steadiest paycheck.
body_markdown:
Sixty-nine point four degrees at New London, seventy point nine at Kings Point — that gradient tells you everything about why the bass have gone quiet on top this week. Warm surface water like that pushes big stripers off the boils and down onto the bottom third of the water column, and that's exactly where I found them Tuesday working Valiant Rock on the last two hours of the ebb, wire line out 250 feet, tube-and-worm dragging bottom in 45 feet of water while the current ran a modest 3.6 knots over the rock. That's soft for The Race in August — we've seen it push 5 in a hard new-moon ebb — but soft current with warm water on top means the fish are stacked tight to structure instead of spread across the whole rip, and that made for a slower pick but a quality one: two fish over 30 pounds came off the wire in about ninety minutes of dragging, both right in the seam where the rock breaks the flow.

Slack at Valiant this week has been sliding into the late morning, drifting close to fifty minutes later each day as we come off the moon — that short window, maybe fifteen minutes either side of dead slack, is when I'll switch off the wire and throw bucktails. Four-ounce white and chartreuse, bounced slow along the bottom right as the current dies, has been picking up a few fish that the trollers miss because they're set up too shallow. Once the current builds back past 2 knots on the new flood, I'm back on wire, because that's when the bait gets pinned against the rock and the bass turn on.

Honest read: this isn't a blitz week. The daytime bite in the open Sound has that typical late-summer flatness to it — warm, calm, not much showing on top. If you want consistency right now, Plum Gut and the Sluiceway are where I'd send you. Black sea bass have been the steadiest thing going, stacked on the humps in 50 to 60 feet on the Gut side, taking squid strips and Gulp on half-ounce bucktails dropped straight down on the last of the ebb. Keeper-sized fish, good numbers, and it fills the box when the bass aren't cooperating. Fluke through the same water have been lazy — that warm layer on top does that to them — so I've had better luck fishing bigger baits, whole squid strips over a 4-inch Gulp Swimming Mullet on a 3/4-ounce bucktail, dragged dead slow tight to the bottom contour rather than working it aggressively. Warm-water fluke want the bait to come to them.

We flagged the snapper blue pattern building two weeks back, and it's arrived right on schedule — the mouth of the Thames is stacked with them right now, along with a real showing of adult 3- to 5-pound blues mixing into the bait pushing through Race Rock at first light. Small metal, half-ounce Deadly Dicks or Kastmasters, worked fast on the surface at dawn before the sun gets up, has been the move. Those adults are following the same peanut bunker schools that have been triggering the daylight blitzes further up the coast, and I'd expect that class of bluefish to keep building through the Race and into Plum Gut as more bait funnels through on the building tide cycle.

No albies yet, and I'm not going to tell you otherwise. Nantucket Sound and the Cape are seeing early bonito activity and there's been enough warm water sitting off Chatham to push some exotic fish into range, which tells me the false albacore push toward eastern Long Island Sound is probably a couple weeks out rather than days. I'll be watching Little Gull Island and Great Gull Island closely once we get into the last week of August — that's historically where the first fall run of albies and bonito show up in this zone, working bait pinned against the rips on a hard current. Right now those spots are quiet, holding bluefish and the occasional straggler bass, nothing worth a special trip yet.

Looking ahead: tides are building back toward the August 28 full moon, and that's the variable that matters most for the next ten days. As current speed climbs back toward 4-plus knots at Race Rock and Valiant, expect the bass to spread back out across the rip instead of holding tight to structure — that's when the wire-line trolling really opens up again, and it's also when I'd expect the first real push of bait and predator fish to move through the Gull Island rips. If the moon does what it usually does to this stretch of water, by the 25th or so we should see current strength and bait density both spike together, and that combination is what turns a grind-it-out week like this one into a proper Race bite. Until then, I'd fish the slack windows on bucktails, save the wire for the building current, and lean on Plum Gut sea bass to keep the day from being a skunk.
